This is already a thoughtfully engineered agent environment. I would evolve it into a shared core with thin vendor adapters—not try to reproduce Claude’s entire plugin stack in GPT/Codex.

What I found:

- Callisto is a 10-crate Rust release engine with strong boundaries: permissive `model`/`format`/`vcs`, CST-preserving manifest edits, atomic writes, `miette` diagnostics, and `just`/Moon verification.
- `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` give a solid shared operational baseline.
- Claude adds:
  - Entire lifecycle hooks and checkpoints;
  - durable `.claude/specs`, plans, semantic-model docs, and handoff state;
  - eight enabled Orin DX plugins (`vector`, `axiom`, `canon`, `delta`, `graph`, `lambda`, `proof`, `trace`);
  - a portable local Rust bug-hunter workflow under `.agents`, plus a local plugin bundle.
- Entire is installed, but `entire status` reports Claude hooks are out of date and only detects Claude/Gemini—not Codex—so there is currently no GPT lifecycle parity.
- Your global Codex default is already sensible: `gpt-5.6-terra` with `medium` reasoning. That’s the right baseline for daily repository work; reserve higher effort for design/audit gates.

My recommendation, in priority order:

1. Make `AGENTS.md` the durable cross-agent contract. Keep only stable rules there: architecture, ownership/licensing boundaries, edit safety, task runner commands, validation expectations, and approval limits. Avoid duplicating it in Claude/Codex files.

2. Add a small repo-local Codex adapter (`.codex/`) with:
   - trusted-project settings;
   - project model/reasoning defaults only if you want this repo to override global defaults;
   - lifecycle hooks that invoke Entire, once its current CLI confirms Codex support;
   - no duplicate prose rules.

3. Promote the useful workflows, not the Claude plugin names:
   - Preserve the Rust bug-hunter as a Codex skill; it is already detected here from `.agents/skills/bug-hunter`.
   - Create two compact Callisto-specific skills: `spec-plan-execute` (consume `.claude/specs` and plans safely) and `release-invariants` (CST/atomic/licensing/diagnostic checks).
   - Do not port the eight enabled Claude plugins blind: their settings only name them; their actual manifests/instructions are not in this repo, so their behavior cannot yet be audited or mapped faithfully.

4. Treat `.claude/specs`, `.claude/plans`, and `.claude/semantic-model` as agent-neutral project artifacts. Codex can use them directly. The current active work appears to be SPEC-007: GitHub release binary assets, with 12 planned slices and 20 acceptance criteria.

5. Trim repeated prompt material. GPT’s official guidance specifically favors one authoritative instruction, task-specific tools, and lean prompts; repeated policies make long runs slower and noisier. Yes. I can work from all of it, and I’ve now indexed the full 312k-word artifact set; read the design, architecture, workflow, security, semantic-model, handoff, and current implementation seams; and extracted the structured goals/criteria from every spec and plan. The important conclusion is that Callisto’s engineering is stronger than its current documentation system makes it appear.

The product position is real:

| Tool | Where Callisto wins | Where it must not overclaim |
|---|---|---|
| Changesets | Native Rust, Cargo/npm/Python coordination, CST-preserving writes, napi platform-package model | Changesets remains the mature default for JS-only repos, with a very familiar contributor workflow and fixed/linked package semantics. [Changesets](https://changesets.dev/guide/getting-started), [configuration](https://changesets.dev/guide/config) |
| Knope | Dependency graph/cascade semantics, range preservation, richer diagnostics, native napi coordination | Knope already supports Changesets-compatible files, multiple versioned files per package, Cargo workspaces, npm, and Python version files; its gaps are more specific than the docs imply. Its Python dependency rewriting remains unsupported. [Knope changesets](https://knope.tech/reference/concepts/changeset/), [package support](https://knope.tech/reference/config-file/packages/) |
| Release Please | Explicit intent files, cross-ecosystem identity, stronger apply/plan model | Release Please has a mature GitHub Release PR workflow, manifest state, workspace plugins, linked versions, and group priority. Its Cargo workspace plugin builds a dependency graph and updates dependents/lockfiles. [Release Please manifest releaser](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please/blob/main/docs/manifest-releaser.md) |
| Nx Release | Build-system-neutral CLI/WASM path, manifest roles, napi edge cases | Nx already has fixed/independent release groups, dependent cascades across groups, version plans, build-before-versioning, and multi-ecosystem publishing. It is the default for Nx users. [Nx Release](https://nx.dev/docs/guides/nx-release), [release groups](https://nx.dev/docs/guides/nx-release/release-groups) |

My highest-confidence recommendations:

1. Establish an authoritative current-state layer.

`docs/00-design.md` calls itself canonical, but correctly admits Python shipped ahead of its own design. The semantic model is more concerning: it still describes already-fixed bugs as current—for example, changeset staging and git-version wiring—and says package-set diagnostics are never emitted even though the current walker emits them.

Keep specs immutable, but add a short maintained `docs/current-state.md` with:

- shipped capability matrix by ecosystem;
- explicitly deferred capabilities;
- current CLI/JSON schema contracts;
- active release workflow;
- links to the governing spec or implementation test.

Then add a CI doc-drift check for claims such as “planned,” “unimplemented,” “never emitted,” and “known gap.” This is the clearest DX improvement available.

2. Make plans first-class, durable release artifacts.

The semantic model identifies the right gap: `VersionPlan` is serializable but not persisted. Current tagging accepts a persisted `PublishPlan`, but versioning/publishing still recompute parts of state. That leaves retry semantics more complex than they need to be after an interrupted version/apply/publish run.

A future “release transaction” should persist:

```text
plan → validate fresh preconditions → apply → publish outcomes → tag outcomes
```

Not a database; a versioned JSON plan plus a resumable outcome journal is enough. This would close the largest reliability/DX gap versus Release Please and Nx.

3. Decide whether releases are signed or merely SHA-verified.

The documentation describes signed tags, but the implementation deliberately disables GPG signing when creating tags for robustness. SHA verification is valuable, but it is not tag-signature verification. Pick one contract:

- enforce verified signed tags in release CI; or
- document unsigned, SHA-anchored release tags precisely.

That is a documentation/security contract mismatch, not a confirmed vulnerability.

4. Add a “release train” policy or explicitly reject it.

Release Please offers group priority; Nx supports group-specific release behavior. Callisto’s fixed/linked groups solve version alignment, but not the policy question of competing prerelease/stable trains. Define whether one group can block/prioritize another, especially around prereleases and GitHub releases.

5. Make performance a product claim with benchmarks.

The architecture has good foundations: native Git integration, cached manifest access, topological planning, and a recent optimization avoiding repeated publish-plan scans. But there is no durable performance suite that demonstrates:

- cold/warm workspace discovery;
- plan/apply time at 10, 100, and 1,000 packages;
- memory use;
- no-regression thresholds.

For a release engine claiming speed, Criterion-style benchmarks plus representative polyglot fixtures are more persuasive than prose.

6. Preserve the current security posture, then harden supply chain boundaries.

The codebase is already unusually disciplined here:

- path containment guards;
- permit-based dry-run write blocking;
- atomic replacement and fsync;
- registry allowlisting for `publishConfig.registry`;
- credential redaction in live and diagnostic output;
- diagnostic-rich errors.

The next security increment should be provenance, not more ad hoc validation:

- provenance/attestation outputs for publish plans and assets;
- optional trusted-tag policy;
- explicit registry URL normalization policy;
- an integration test matrix for malicious manifest/config inputs.

I did not identify a new confirmed vulnerability; the atomic-write parent-directory `sync_all` errors are intentionally ignored, so I would classify that as an unverified crash-durability risk worth a fault-injection test—not a confirmed finding.

For Codex/GPT specifically, I’d now add three compact skills, rather than more global prompt text:

- `callisto-release-transaction`: plan/apply/publish/tag state, idempotency, partial-failure handling.
- `callisto-spec-drift`: compare docs/semantic models/specs against code and tests before changing contracts.
- `callisto-competitive-positioning`: use only when editing README/docs/product direction, to prevent stale competitor claims.

Also, retain `AGENTS.md` as the sole durable engineering contract. The `.codex` Entire adapter is installed, but the repository currently has no project-local Codex skills beyond the existing bug-hunter workflow; the two earlier proposed skills are no longer in the worktree, so they should be reintroduced only once the concurrent work is settled.

The most valuable next concrete task is a read-only “documentation authority and drift” spec: define which file owns each claim, enumerate currently stale claims, and add a cheap CI guard. It improves contributor DX, GPT/Codex reliability, and product credibility simultaneously.

The mistake here is treating completed specs and semantic models as museum pieces. That creates exactly the failure mode you’re worried about: future people and agents read a confident “known bug” or “planned” statement and make the wrong change.

I’d use this hierarchy:

| Artifact | Role | Update policy |
|---|---|---|
| `docs/01-spec.md` | Normative product/architecture contract | Update whenever the intended contract changes or implementation proves a prior claim wrong |
| `docs/00-design.md` | Product rationale and boundaries | Update when positioning, ecosystem scope, or architectural decisions evolve |
| `.claude/specs/*.json` | Acceptance criteria for a feature | Amend when discovery invalidates a criterion; record a concise correction note |
| `.claude/plans/*.json` | Execution plan | Update status and revise tasks when implementation exposes a wrong assumption |
| `.claude/semantic-model/*` | Fast operational reference for agents | Keep synchronized with code; it must never knowingly describe fixed bugs as current |
| `SESSION_HANDOFF.md` | Historical session context | Mark superseded sections clearly rather than treating it as current authority |

I would not create a separate `current-state.md` as a workaround for stale specs. That would introduce yet another source of truth. Instead, fix the existing sources and add a compact index that says which artifacts are normative versus historical.

The concrete maintenance track should:

1. Correct known drift: Python’s shipped status, fixed staging/git-version/package-set behavior, current publish/tag semantics, and current identity/promotion behavior.
2. Resolve contradictory publishing language: Callisto orchestrates publishing through ecosystem CLIs; it does not implement registry protocols itself.
3. Add `status`, `last_verified_commit`, and `supersedes`/`superseded_by` fields to specs and plans where useful.
4. Add a CI check that rejects stale markers such as “planned,” “never emitted,” or “known bug” when a linked regression test or code path shows otherwise.
5. Require every behavior-changing PR to update the governing spec and semantic-model entry in the same change.

That is a better GPT/Codex setup too: it gives agents a truthful, layered contract instead of asking them to reconcile historical prose with current code on every task.
GIve me more details on the 2-4 above, durable plans, SHA, etc. I want to understand what you're proposing

## 2. Durable plans

Today, Callisto has the right internal shape but an incomplete handoff:

```text
changesets/config/git
        ↓
   VersionPlan
        ↓ apply
manifests/changelogs/changesets

workspace state
        ↓
   PublishPlan JSON
        ↓ publish / tag
registries + GitHub releases
```

`VersionPlan` already describes the intended version changes, dependency rewrites, changelog writes, consumed changesets, and pre-mode updates. But it is computed and immediately applied; it is not a durable artifact a later command can validate and resume. `PublishPlan` is closer—it is JSON and `tag` can consume it—but publish planning can still be recomputed from a workspace whose state may have changed.

What I propose is an optional, explicit release-plan workflow:

```text
callisto plan version --output release-plan.json
callisto apply --plan release-plan.json
callisto plan publish --from release-plan.json --output publish-plan.json
callisto publish --plan publish-plan.json
callisto tag --plan publish-plan.json
```

Each plan would contain:

- schema version;
- workspace root and Git commit SHA;
- digest of relevant config and input changesets;
- expected `from` versions and intended `to` versions;
- ordered mutations and publish operations;
- the diagnostics observed during planning.

Before applying, Callisto would re-check that the workspace still matches the plan’s preconditions. If it does not, it refuses instead of silently applying a stale plan.

This is not a database or hidden mutable state. The plan can be a CI artifact, a checked-in release-PR artifact, or an ignored local file. Its value is human review, reproducibility, and recovery after a partial failure.

For example, if npm publish succeeds, PyPI fails, and the job dies before tags are created, a resume command can report exactly what is already done and retry only what is safe. That is materially better than rerunning a broad release command and hoping every downstream CLI is idempotent.

I would make this opt-in at first. Normal `callisto version` remains ergonomic; production automation uses plans.

## 3. SHA verification vs signed tags

These solve different problems.

A tag name is a pointer:

```text
callisto-cli@0.5.0  ──► commit 627039c4
```

A SHA is the immutable identity of the commit content:

```text
627039c4…  = exactly one Git object
```

Verifying a release tag resolves to the expected SHA ensures the release job acts on the same source that was versioned and approved. It prevents mistakes such as checking out one commit, creating/reading a tag that resolves elsewhere, then publishing mismatched source.

But SHA verification does not answer: “who authorized this tag?”

A cryptographic tag signature, such as GPG or SSH signing, answers that identity question if CI verifies it against trusted keys. Current Callisto code intentionally disables GPG signing while generating tags, so the documentation should not imply signed-tag enforcement exists.

There are three valid policies:

1. SHA-anchored, unsigned tags

   Best default for ease of use. CI verifies tag-to-commit consistency and protected branches/tags control who can push. Documentation says exactly that.

2. Optional trusted signatures

   A `require-signed-tags` policy for security-sensitive repositories. CI verifies the tag signature against an allowlist. This is stronger, but key distribution, rotation, bot signing, and local developer UX become product responsibilities.

3. GitHub-native provenance

   Rely on protected tags plus GitHub Actions identity, artifact attestations, and immutable/draft GitHub releases. This is often more practical than individual GPG keys for modern CI releases.

My recommendation is policy 1 now, with a clean extension point for policy 2. Correct the docs immediately; do not impose signing before there is a real customer/security requirement.

## 4. Release trains / group priority

Fixed and linked groups answer:

> Which packages must align their versions?

They do not answer:

> Which release should proceed when multiple release streams are pending?

Example:

```text
stable releases:     cli, graph
prerelease releases: moon beta, native bindings beta
```

A group-priority policy can say:

```text
If beta train has pending work, prepare only beta.
Otherwise prepare stable.
```

Release Please exposes this as `group-priority`. Nx solves related concerns with release groups and group-specific behavior. This prevents a single release PR from mixing a beta line with a stable line when that would confuse consumers or registry channels.

For Callisto, there are three choices:

- Explicitly reject the feature for now: one release flow at a time; document that fixed/linked groups are not release lanes.
- Add lightweight lanes later: a named lane selects packages, version channel, tag template, registry dist-tag, and exclusivity/priority.
- Build a general scheduler now: flexible but much more configuration, testing, and operational complexity.

I recommend the first choice now, while writing down the boundary clearly. The second becomes worthwhile only when Callisto has a real multi-channel user—not merely because competitors expose it.

Priority order: durable plans are a genuine near-term reliability advantage; SHA/signing clarification is a low-cost security/documentation correction; release lanes are a deliberate future product decision.
When the plan is running in CI how do we best handle this? Is there a problem to checking in files that we can forget to clean up? Should it be cached by GH instead?

Use GitHub Actions artifacts, not Git-tracked plan files and not the GitHub cache.

A cache is the wrong primitive: it is evictable, mutable, optimized for speed rather than integrity, and can be unavailable exactly when a release needs recovery. A checked-in `release-plan.json` is durable but creates cleanup debt and makes ordinary release PRs noisy.

The clean model is:

```text
Version PR
  └─ computes VersionPlan
  └─ applies it
  └─ commits manifests, changelogs, consumed changesets
  └─ uploads plan.json as a CI artifact for review/debugging

Merged version commit / release tag
  └─ verifies exact commit SHA
  └─ computes PublishPlan
  └─ uploads publish-plan.json immediately as an artifact
  └─ publishes in order
  └─ creates tags/releases
```

The committed versioned files are already the durable cross-workflow record. The plan artifact is supporting evidence: it explains exactly why those files changed and lets reviewers inspect the proposed operations before side effects begin.

For partial publish failure, do not rely on a cached or committed “success checkpoint.” Query the authoritative systems on retry:

- registry state: is `package@version` already published?
- Git state: does the release tag point to the expected SHA?
- GitHub state: does the release/release asset already exist?

Then retry only the unfinished idempotent operations. This aligns with Callisto’s existing design principle: state may be a hint, but correctness comes from disk, Git, registries, and GitHub.

The plan artifact should be uploaded immediately after planning—not only at workflow end—so it survives a later failure. It should contain a digest and source commit SHA, and later stages should reject it if either no longer matches.

For normal CI:

- Use job outputs only for small values: plan SHA-256, source SHA, artifact name/run ID.
- Use `upload-artifact` / `download-artifact` for the full JSON plan between jobs.
- Set a moderate retention period, such as 30–90 days.
- Put a concise plan summary and digest into the GitHub job summary or release PR body.

For a manual recovery days later, regenerate the plan from the already-versioned commit, then reconcile it with registry/tag/release reality. That is safer than trusting an old artifact or cache.

So: artifacts for observability and intra-run handoff; committed manifests/changelogs for release intent; external systems for recovery truth.

Treat source identity and authorization as separate, provider-independent layers.

```text
Callisto core:
  “What exact source am I releasing?”
  → commit SHA + plan/config/input digests

CI/forge adapter:
  “Who is allowed to authorize this release?”
  → protected refs, approvals, OIDC identity, signatures/attestations
```

The core should never depend on GitHub. Bazel is a build system rather than a forge, but it fits naturally: it builds an exact Git commit and emits provenance; GitHub, GitLab, Buildkite, Jenkins, or a local runner can provide the authorization layer.

## Core release binding

Every generated release plan should carry:

```json
{
  "sourceCommit": "627039c4...",
  "configDigest": "sha256:...",
  "inputDigest": "sha256:...",
  "schemaVersion": 1
}
```

At every side-effect boundary, Callisto verifies:

1. The checked-out `HEAD` equals `sourceCommit`.
2. `callisto.toml` and release inputs match their expected digests.
3. A newly created package tag resolves to `sourceCommit`.
4. A pre-existing tag either resolves to that same SHA or fails closed.

This works everywhere Git works. It protects against stale plans, checkout/ref confusion, and tag/commit mismatches. It does not prove who authorized the release.

## GitHub setup

For GitHub Actions, I would use:

- A protected `main` branch and protected release-tag patterns, such as `*@*`.
- A protected GitHub Environment named `release`, with required reviewer approval and scoped secrets.
- Least-privilege `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions; grant `contents: write` only in the release job.
- Pin every third-party action to a commit SHA.
- Trigger releases only from a protected branch, protected tag, or explicit manual dispatch.
- Check out the exact planned SHA, not a moving branch name.
- Upload the plan and its digest as an artifact before publishing.
- Create a draft release, attach artifacts, then publish it after all assets are present.

Conceptually:

```yaml
release:
  environment: release
  permissions:
    contents: write
    id-token: write
  steps:
    - checkout exact sourceCommit
    - verify HEAD == sourceCommit
    - download and verify publish-plan.json
    - publish packages
    - create tags and verify each resolves to sourceCommit
    - create draft release, upload assets, publish release
```

`id-token: write` enables GitHub OIDC. Use it for keyless artifact provenance/signing where the registry or artifact format supports it; do not put a long-lived signing key in repository secrets.

## Signed tags: optional, not the default

Signed tags are useful only when you have a credible trust policy:

```text
Require tag signature
  → verify tag against a configured trusted key/identity set
  → then verify tag resolves to the planned SHA
```

For human-operated releases, GPG or SSH Git signatures work well.

For CI-created tags, forcing GPG signing is often awkward: you must operate and rotate a bot key, secure it, and make all environments trust it. In that case, GitHub OIDC-backed provenance is generally a better signal than a bot-owned GPG key.

So I would support policy modes:

```toml
[release.provenance]
source-sha = "require"          # portable core behavior
git-signature = "optional"      # verify if present, do not require
```

Later, a security-sensitive organization could set:

```toml
git-signature = "require"
trusted-signers = ["ssh:...", "gpg:..."]
```

Callisto would invoke standard Git verification rather than inventing cryptography.

## Non-GitHub / Bazel

The portable contract stays the same:

```text
CI obtains a trusted source SHA
→ Callisto plans/releases only that SHA
→ CI signs or attests the built artifacts
→ registry/Git release state is reconciled on retry
```

Examples:

- GitLab: protected branches/tags, protected environments, OIDC workload identity.
- Buildkite/Jenkins: restricted release pipeline, short-lived cloud credentials, signed build provenance.
- Bazel: build with an explicitly pinned source revision; produce a provenance statement tying artifact digest, build command, and source SHA together.
- Local release: require an explicit SHA and optionally a Git-signature verification command.

The right abstraction is a `sourceCommit` requirement in Callisto plus forge-specific policy in the workflow. That gives every environment the same correctness guarantees without making GitHub’s model part of the release engine.

The core implementation has a strong security posture; the biggest residual risk is release-pipeline trust, not ordinary Rust memory safety or manifest handling.

## What is strong

- Safe Rust is enforced workspace-wide.
- Write-capable operations require an `ApplyPermit`, so dry-run paths cannot accidentally mutate disk.
- Manifest/config paths are constrained to the workspace; TOML/JSON edits preserve structure; writes use temp-file replacement plus file sync.
- Apply is guarded by expected `from`/`to` versions, preventing a stale plan from overwriting an unexpected manifest state.
- Registry publishing is unusually well defended:
  - `publishConfig.registry` must be HTTPS and exactly match an operator-configured registry;
  - publish-target ecosystem mismatches fail closed;
  - subprocess output has a 10 MiB capture cap;
  - known credentials and URL userinfo are redacted from live output and diagnostics.
- The dependency audit completed successfully: no active RustSec advisory was reported for the resolved lockfile, and unknown registries/Git sources are denied in [deny.toml](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/deny.toml).

## Confirmed security concerns

1. Release credentials run automatically on every push to `main`.

The release job has `contents`, PR, check, and status write permissions and receives Cargo/npm tokens; it triggers on every push to `main` with no GitHub Environment approval gate. See [callisto-release.yml](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml).

That can be acceptable only if branch protection is exceptionally strong. Otherwise, any malicious or compromised merged code can execute with registry credentials.

Recommendation: move actual publishing to a protected `release` Environment requiring approval, and trigger publishing from a protected tag or explicit dispatch—not every ordinary `main` push.

2. Third-party GitHub Actions are tag-pinned, not SHA-pinned.

Examples include `actions/checkout@v4`, `taiki-e/install-action@v2`, and toolchain setup actions. Tags are convenient but mutable pointers. A compromised action release can compromise CI, and in the release workflow that means credentials.

Recommendation: pin actions to immutable commit SHAs; use Dependabot/Renovate to maintain them. This is the highest-value supply-chain hardening change.

3. Advisory policy is permissive and not reproducible enough.

The audit passes, but [deny.toml](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/deny.toml) has a broad advisory-ignore list for Wasmtime-related test dependencies and explicitly describes advisory DB results as unstable. Today’s run says those ignored advisories were not encountered, which is good; however, the policy makes future review harder. The lockfile also contains yanked `bisync 0.3.0`, transitively through `gix`.

Recommendation: update/remove the yanked dependency when upstream permits it, pin the advisory database revision or otherwise make CI’s advisory input reproducible, and give every advisory exception an owner and expiry/review date.

## Important design risks, not confirmed vulnerabilities

- Release tags are SHA-related but not signature-enforced. The docs should say “SHA-anchored” unless CI verifies trusted Git signatures.
- File writes are atomically durable per file, but a multi-file version operation is not one filesystem transaction. The idempotency checks make retries safe, but a durable plan/outcome model would improve recovery and auditability.
- Per-crate coverage is currently warning-only; security-sensitive crates should not rely solely on the aggregate 90% threshold.

## Recommended order

1. Protect publishing with a GitHub Environment, approval, and least-privilege release permissions.
2. Pin every external action by commit SHA.
3. Make release plans SHA-bound and upload them as artifacts before side effects.
4. Clarify unsigned-vs-signed tag policy; add optional signature verification later.
5. Tighten dependency/audit reproducibility and retire the yanked `bisync` path.
6. Add fault-injection tests for partial release recovery and failed directory sync.

I would rate the code-level posture as strong, the dependency posture as acceptable but needing cleanup, and the current release workflow as the main high-impact hardening target.

content.text:
I found several merge-blocking release and security issues on current `a372dced`. This was read-only; no files changed.

### [High] Release workflow invokes a CLI command that does not exist

- **Status**: CONFIRMED
- **Location**: [.github/actions/callisto-action/action.yml](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/action.yml:222), [cli.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/src/cli.rs:36)
- **Classification**: CI integration / silent release failure
- **Root cause**: The action calls `callisto filter-plan`, but no `FilterPlan` subcommand or implementation exists.
- **Failing scenario**: Any normal `publish: true` release reaches this line after publishing. The action exits there, leaving successfully published packages untagged and without releases.
- **Verification strategy**: An integration test must invoke the compiled `callisto` binary—not a stub—and assert that the action’s command set exists.

### [High] Workflow expects `isFloatingMajor`, but `TagReport` never emits it

- **Status**: CONFIRMED
- **Location**: [action.yml](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/action.yml:251), [report.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/report.rs:611), [tag.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/tag.rs:64)
- **Classification**: Release correctness / spec-wire drift
- **Root cause**: The workflow filters tags using `.isFloatingMajor`, while `CreatedTag` only has `package`, `tagName`, `sha`, and `alreadyExisted`.
- **Failing scenario**: Both jq selections produce no tags, so local tags are created but neither immutable nor floating tags are pushed. Existing shell tests incorrectly provide an invented `isFloatingMajor` field in stubbed JSON.
- **Verification strategy**: Generate a real `TagReport` and assert the workflow categorizes and pushes both tag kinds.

### [High] Tag failure does not stop GitHub-release creation

- **Status**: CONFIRMED
- **Location**: [action.yml](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/action.yml:239)
- **Classification**: Partial-failure integrity
- **Root cause**: A failed `callisto tag` only emits `::error::`; execution continues into `gh release create`.
- **Failing scenario**: A tag conflict or Git failure can still create a GitHub Release, potentially causing GitHub to create/reference a tag that was not created at the planned SHA.
- **Verification strategy**: Stub `callisto tag` to fail and assert no `gh release create` is executed and the job exits non-zero.

### [High] Publish planning converts versioning/Git failures into warnings, then publishes

- **Status**: CONFIRMED
- **Location**: [publish.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/publish.rs:218), [publish.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/publish.rs:234), [publish.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/publish.rs:100)
- **Classification**: Silent fallback / release integrity
- **Root cause**: `plan_publish` catches all `plan_version` and Git-discovery errors, emits warnings, and continues constructing publish entries from current manifests.
- **Failing scenario**: A malformed changeset, graph-planning failure, or Git/tag-read failure can result in registry publication without a valid version plan or release-tag entry.
- **Verification strategy**: A fixture with an invalid changeset or failed Git read must make `plan-publish`/`publish` fail before registry commands run.

### [High] Symlinked package discovery can escape the workspace

- **Status**: CONFIRMED
- **Location**: [ignore_walk.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/ignore_walk.rs:39), [ignore_walk.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/ignore_walk.rs:155), [walk.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/walk.rs:180)
- **Classification**: Filesystem-boundary security
- **Root cause**: Discovery deliberately follows symlinked directories, but validates the lexical symlink path rather than its canonical target. Later manifest writes and publisher subprocesses follow that link outside the workspace.
- **Failing scenario**: A repository symlink can cause `version` to edit an external manifest or `publish` to run package-manager lifecycle code from an external directory. This is especially concerning in the privileged release workflow.
- **Verification strategy**: Create a symlink inside a fixture workspace to an external package directory; discovery must reject it or require an explicit, canonicalized allowlist.

### [Medium] Malformed workspace membership fails open

- **Status**: CONFIRMED
- **Location**: [membership.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/membership.rs:19), [membership.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/membership.rs:270)
- **Classification**: Silent fallback / unexpected publish scope
- **Root cause**: Invalid Cargo, pnpm, or npm workspace metadata becomes an absent membership filter, which admits every discovered manifest.
- **Failing scenario**: A malformed `pnpm-workspace.yaml` can make unrelated `package.json` files eligible for graph inclusion and release planning.
- **Verification strategy**: Invalid membership metadata should produce a diagnostic error and no publishable graph, rather than an admit-all graph.

### [Medium] `--refresh-lockfiles` reports failures but exits successfully

- **Status**: CONFIRMED

Yes. The audit findings are real, but two are currently a PR-stack integration failure rather than defects in #29’s intended code.

| PR | Validation | Required action |
|---|---|---|
| #29 `filter-plan` primitives | Contains the missing `filter-plan` CLI and `CreatedTag.isFloatingMajor`; CI is green. But its release filtering is incomplete: a release remains if no matching publish attempt exists. | Fix before merge. |
| #30 runner/action fixes | Independent and clean; it does not address release-plan semantics. | Can merge independently after normal review. |
| #31 action orchestration | Uses #29 APIs but is based on #30, not #29. Therefore it currently compiles/runs against a binary without those APIs/fields. | Do not merge as-is. Rebase after #29 and #30 land, or create an explicit integration branch containing both. |
| #32 specs | Correct long-term direction, but does not yet capture every immediate regression condition below. | Add the release-state contract details before implementation begins. |

The stack should be:

1. Fix and merge #29.
2. Merge #30.
3. Rebase #31 onto the resulting `main`.
4. Add an integration test using the real compiled CLI and real report schema—not shell stubs.
5. Only then enable/merge the release action change.

The key defect in #29 is in `filter_plan_by_report`: package publish lists are retained only when a successful attempt exists, but `releases` are retained whenever no failed attempt matches. “Not attempted” therefore incorrectly counts as release-safe. The semantic rule must be:

> A release entry is eligible for tagging only if every planned publish operation for that release has a matching successful or already-published attempt, at the planned version.

No attempt, mismatched version, duplicate contradictory attempts, or failed attempt must all make it ineligible.

Architecturally, this should not remain a set of parallel vectors plus shell/jq interpretation. `PublishPlan` currently has crate/npm/PyPI vectors and a separate `releases` vector; the relationship is inferred from package names. That is why the filter bug exists.

I recommend introducing a model-owned release unit:

```text
ReleaseUnit
  id
  package identity
  source SHA
  version
  required publish operations [operation IDs]
  tag operation
  changelog/release metadata
```

`PublishReport` should report outcomes by `operation_id`, not reconstruct identity from bare package names. Then `callisto-graph` owns one deterministic projection:

```text
PublishPlan + PublishReport -> ReconciledReleasePlan
```

The GitHub Action should only execute that projection and perform adapter-side actions. It should not decide what shipped with jq.

Immediate release behavior should be:

- A tag failure is fatal; do not create a GitHub Release afterward.
- A tag push failure is fatal; do not create a GitHub Release afterward.
- `gh release create` failure is fatal unless an explicit idempotent “already exists and targets expected tag” result is verified.
- A successful package publish with an incomplete release unit is recorded for reconciliation, not silently treated as a completed release.
- Release output must distinguish `planned`, `published`, `tagged-local`, `tagged-remote`, `release-created`, `failed`, and `reconcile-required`.

For the other audit findings, I would split ownership this way:

| Concern | Correct owner | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| Plan/report/release matching | `callisto-model` + `callisto-graph` | Add operation and release-unit identity; enforce reconciliation invariants. |
| CLI JSON boundaries | `callisto-cli` | Validate schema version and plan provenance before tag/publish execution. |
| Git/tag behavior | `callisto-vcs` | Add source-SHA preconditions and report real remote/tag state. |
| Workspace filesystem boundary | `callisto-model` | Introduce a workspace-root capability, then require it for manifest/changelog writes and publishing cwd resolution. |
| Discovery/membership | `callisto-graph` | Fail closed on malformed membership metadata; reject symlink targets outside the workspace by default. |
| Atomic write durability | `callisto-model` | Propagate parent-directory fsync errors as “committed but durability uncertain,” never success. |
| Lock refresh | `callisto-graph` | Make failure explicit and non-zero; follow with a journaled workspace-mutation transaction for clean rollback/recovery. |
| GitHub authorization | workflow adapter | Protected environment, least permissions, SHA-pinned actions, explicit artifact handoff. |

For the symlink problem, the existing `workspace_relative` model is syntactic, not a real filesystem boundary. A capability-based filesystem API such as [`cap-std`](https://docs.rs/cap-std/latest/cap_std/fs/index.html) is worth evaluating: it operates relative to an opened directory capability rather than arbitrary paths. I would use it selectively for mutation paths first—manifest, changelog, changeset, and plan-artifact I/O—rather than rewrite all discovery at once.

For Cargo membership, avoid duplicating Cargo’s workspace semantics. `cargo metadata --format-version 1 --no-deps` is the authoritative source for workspace members; Cargo explicitly documents it as machine-readable workspace metadata. [Cargo metadata](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/cargo/commands/cargo-metadata.html) For npm/Python, malformed membership configuration should produce a diagnostic error, not broaden to admit-all discovery.

I would add two CI tools:

- [`actionlint`](https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint/blob/main/docs/usage.md) for workflow syntax/expression validation.
- [`zizmor`](https://docs.zizmor.sh/quickstart/) for GitHub Actions security checks, including permissions and risky workflow patterns. It can emit SARIF for code scanning. [Integration guidance](https://docs.zizmor.sh/integrations/)

Most importantly, add a release-adapter integration test that builds the actual Callisto binary and runs the composite action in a temporary Git repository with a local bare remote. That test should cover:

1. success;
2. one publish failure;
3. no publish attempt;
4. tag conflict;
5. remote push failure;
6. existing GitHub Release;
7. source SHA mismatch;
8. rerun/reconciliation.

That closes the gap that allowed #31’s shell tests to validate invented JSON fields and a nonexistent command.

### Critical — 001/002/003 now contradict each other

The repository confirms Claude’s summary: 005 has a real implementation branch; 001A/B/C, 002–004, and 006 are still specs/design work, not shipped code or workflow changes. The key decision to stop autonomous iteration on the release tracks is correct.

## Current verdict

- **005 documentation authority:** close, but not ready to land yet.
- **001A/001B/001C:** should not be implemented until the execution boundary and model ownership are settled together.
- **004:** needs one authoritative audit database design; its current draft would otherwise audit and record different database states.
- **006:** needs an aggregate-conflict diagnostic design.
- **Existing release workflow:** still has a high-severity failure-propagation hole that should be included in 001B/001C rather than deferred.

## 005: good implementation, two required corrections

The checker and fixture harness are thoughtfully scoped. The separate authority sets, enrolled-spec metadata, no-rewrite behavior, and omission of plans/handoffs are all solid.

Claude correctly found the missing cross-glob test: the harness tests invalid values in `docs/*.md`, but not that `normative`/`guide` are rejected in `.claude/semantic-model/*.md`, nor that `verified-current` is rejected in `docs/*.md`. Add that test.

There is one additional compliance gap: `just ci` and `just ci-fast` run `lint-docs`, but the actual GitHub CI workflow invokes `just lint`, `just test`, etc. individually—never `just ci` or `just lint-docs`. Thus the authority rule is not currently CI-enforced. [Justfile](<https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/codex/005-doc-authority-v2/justfile>) vs. [CI workflow](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/workflows/callisto-ci.yml:35).

Recommendation: add a lightweight `docs-authority` CI job running `just lint-docs`, then land 005.

## 001A: Claude found a real layering problem

The spec assigns envelope/digest computation to `callisto-model`, but the required inputs—resolved config, workspace membership, package discovery, dependency edges—belong to `callisto-graph`. Moving collection into model would reverse the dependency boundary and create a cycle.

The clean split is:

- `callisto-model`: envelope data types, canonical serialization, SHA-256, structural parsing, and comparison of already-collected snapshots.
- `callisto-graph`: `collect_release_input_snapshot(workspace)` and validation against the live workspace.
- `callisto-cli`: obtains a validated capability/result and is the only layer allowed to invoke publish/tag mutation.

That preserves the license/layer boundary and avoids duplicate discovery passes.

Claude’s `DepKind` finding is also real: derived `Ord` follows declaration order (`Runtime`, `Dev`, `Peer`, `Optional`, `Build`), not serialized lexical order (`build`, `dev`, `optional`, `peer`, `runtime`). [dependency.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/dependency.rs:9). Do not use derived `Ord` for the digest. Define an explicit canonical string key and sort by that key, with a test over every variant.

## 001B: this is the highest-priority correctness design

Claude’s interrupted-publish concern is confirmed by the current code.

`filter_plan_by_report` defines success as “not failed.” [publish.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/publish.rs:723). If `Planned` or `Attempted` states are added, they would pass that test and allow an unattempted operation to reach tagging/release creation.

The right model is not a boolean helper. It needs:

- Stable **operation identity**: package + version + ecosystem/registry target, not package name alone.
- A closed state machine: `Planned → Attempted → Published|AlreadyPublished|Failed|Skipped`.
- `is_success()`, `is_terminal()`, and `is_complete_for(envelope)` as distinct predicates.
- Filtering that retains a release only when every required operation has a matching terminal success; missing, planned, attempted, failed, duplicate, or mismatched-version entries block it.
- A derived `ReconciledReleasePlan` that binds original envelope digest + report digest + survivor operation IDs. Do not pass an arbitrary newly serialized `PublishPlan` to `tag`.

This is foundational for correct retry, recovery, and “partial publish succeeds” behavior.

Also fold in an existing workflow bug: a tag failure only emits an error, then the action still attempts GitHub releases; `gh release create` is ignored with `|| true`. [action.yml](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/action.yml:239) and [action.yml](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/action.yml:283). A successful publish can therefore yield a successful job despite failed tags/releases. The execute boundary must fail hard at tag push and release creation.

## 001C / 003: the job split is necessary

Claude’s conclusion is right: GitHub Environment approval is job-scoped, so it cannot securely protect a single step inside today’s composite action. The plan job → protected execute job split is necessary to achieve the stated trust boundary.

Two details need explicit decisions before implementation:

- The execute checkout must be pinned to the event SHA or the envelope’s source SHA, then validated before mutation.
- Registry secrets must be scoped only to the post-validation publishing step. Attaching them at job level means they are available before artifact/digest validation, even if the script does not read them.

For empty plans, make the contract unambiguous:

- Plan job outputs `has_operations=false`, uploads no artifact.
- Execute job has `if: needs.plan.outputs.has_operations == 'true'`.
- “Missing artifact is terminal” applies only when execute was intentionally started.

That resolves the current empty-plan contradiction and avoids granting credentials for no work.

## 004: use one audit database, one audit execution

Claude is right that a separate `rustsec::Database::fetch()` cannot prove which advisory database `cargo-deny` actually used. It also makes CI perform two database-fetch/audit paths, which is slower and can produce internally inconsistent results.

The installed cargo-deny supports `--disable-fetch`: fetch/update once in a controlled location, capture that checkout’s revision, then run cargo-deny against that already-fetched state with fetching disabled. The record must describe that exact invocation and database checkout—not a second RustSec client.

Keep this as task-runner/CI tooling, not a new production workspace crate. It avoids inflating Callisto’s shipped dependency graph for CI bookkeeping.

## 006: aggregate conflicts, don’t promise impossible per-package errors

A single `Result<VersionPlan, GraphError>` cannot return a separate error for every qualifying package. The spec should choose one of:

- `PrereleaseGroupConflicts { conflicts: Vec<Conflict> }`, canonically sorted and shown as one diagnostic card; preferred.
- Deterministically return the first conflict, with an explicit sort order; less helpful DX.

The aggregate form gives users every configuration issue in one run and preserves deterministic output.

## Recommended sequence

1. Finish and land 005: cross-glob regression test plus explicit GitHub CI job.
2. Write one short design decision for 001A/001B:
   model-vs-graph ownership, operation identity/state machine, and validated-execution capability.
3. Implement 001A foundation, then 001B report/filter/tag semantics with interruption tests.
4. Implement 001C and 003 together: split jobs, artifact binding, SHA checkout, environment, least privilege, and hard failure propagation.
5. Implement 004 as a single CI wrapper around the exact cargo-deny database/execution.
6. Implement 006 with aggregate diagnostics.

This avoids locking a durable envelope around an unsafe recovery model, which would be much harder to unwind later.

Yes. Looking at it holistically, I would revise the framing before implementing more of 001A–C, 002–004, or 006. The current split finds real problems, but it divides work by CI artifact rather than first establishing Callisto’s release-state model.

The key architectural conclusion is:

```text
Workspace/config ──graph──> immutable ReleaseIntent
                                  │
                         CI artifact / approval
                                  │
source + live config ──graph──> validated execution
                                  │
                             ReleaseReceipt
                                  │
                         reconcile (no mutation)
                                  │
                       eligible tag/release actions
```

This fits Callisto’s existing design: `callisto-model` defines durable semantic values; `callisto-graph` observes and resolves the workspace; `callisto-vcs` observes/mutates Git; CLI and GitHub are adapters. It also resembles the existing version-plan model, which uses semantic `from`/`to` preconditions and atomic application rather than treating a filesystem hash as the entire truth ([version-flow.md](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/semantic-model/version-flow.md:1)).

## The design decisions needed first

1. A plan must be an immutable intent, not a mutable status file.

   Define three separate concepts:

   - `ReleaseIntent`: what was approved to happen, with an exact semantic snapshot.
   - `ReleaseReceipt`: what was actually attempted and its terminal outcome.
   - `ReconciledReleasePlan`: a derived, read-only answer to “which downstream tag/release operations remain eligible?”

   This resolves the interruption bug cleanly. A tag or GitHub release is eligible only when every exact prerequisite operation has a terminal-success receipt—not merely “is not failed.” The present logic can treat unattempted operations as successful, and can retain a release that has no corresponding successful publish attempt ([publish.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/publish.rs:723)).

2. Identity must be exact and operation-level.

   `PackageId::matches` intentionally supports bare-name/wildcard semantics in polyglot contexts. That is useful for selection, but unsafe for authorizing a release operation. The durable model needs an exact `ReleaseOperationId`, including ecosystem, registry target, package identity, version, and operation role.

   A package version might entail Cargo, npm, PyPI, tag, and GitHub-release operations. “Package succeeded” is too weak an invariant.

3. Source binding needs a platform-neutral core and platform-specific evidence.

   A Git commit SHA establishes source identity, not signer identity. Keep these distinct:

   - Core `SourceIdentity`: Git commit, or potentially a content digest for hermetic/non-Git build contexts.
   - Adapter evidence: GitHub attestation, signature, protected-environment approval, etc.
   - Policy: whether evidence is optional, required, or unavailable for a given execution profile.

   This respects the architecture’s stated forge/build-system independence while allowing GitHub’s environment protection to be a strong adapter-level control ([ARCHITECTURE.md](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/ARCHITECTURE.md:360)).

4. The durable artifact must not contain raw registry endpoints.

   This is more serious than the proposed “secret scan.” Existing plan types serialize optional registry/index URLs ([plan.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/plan.rs:59)). A URL can embed credentials in userinfo or query parameters. “It came from repository config rather than environment” does not make it safe to persist in an artifact.

   The intent should carry a stable `RegistryKey`, not a resolved endpoint. Resolve the endpoint only during validated execution, after approval. If an endpoint must be displayed, represent it as a credential-free/redacted type and reject userinfo structurally—not with regex scanning.

5. Canonicalization belongs below graph discovery, but above artifact transport.

   `callisto-model` may own a generic canonical-bytes/digest primitive; it must not discover packages or resolve configuration. `callisto-graph` builds the semantic snapshot and invokes that primitive.

   If the digest is intended to work across Rust, GitHub, Bazel, or other tooling, use RFC 8785/JCS canonical JSON, with a deliberate “no floating point values” rule. [`serde_json_canonicalizer`](https://docs.rs/crate/serde_json_canonicalizer/latest) is a plausible small dependency for that purpose, based on the [JCS standard](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785.html). I would avoid `olpc-cjson`: its own documentation notes that its output can be non-valid JSON, which is a poor fit for a cross-tool release envelope ([documentation](https://docs.rs/olpc-cjson)).

   Also make ordering explicit. `DepKind`’s derived Rust order differs from lexical serialized-name order ([dependency.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/dependency.rs:9)); “sort by kind” is currently not enough to guarantee an identical digest.

## What this means for the current specs

| Area | Reframe needed |
|---|---|
| 001A | Make it the semantic `ReleaseIntent` contract and graph-owned snapshot builder. Remove workspace discovery from `callisto-model`. Define canonicalization, exact operation identities, and secret-safe registry references. |
| 001B | Make it `ReleaseReceipt` plus deterministic reconciliation. Require terminal success and exact prerequisite coverage; never infer success from absence of failure. |
| 001C | Make it a GitHub adapter specification: immutable artifact handoff, checkout at bound source, validation before credentials, environment-gated execution, and an explicit empty-intent contract. |
| 002 | Define a portable source/evidence policy model with named consumers. SHA binding and signature/attestation evidence must not be conflated. |
| 003 | Keep it GitHub-specific. Pin actions, minimize permissions, gate credentials at the execution step, and make tag/release failures fatal. |
| 004 | Use one advisory-database authority and one audit invocation, not a RustSec side path plus a separate `cargo-deny` check. |
| 006 | First settle whether prerelease is workspace-global shaping or explicit release-set membership. Its current roster model is not a safe authorization boundary. |

For 001C specifically, the clean contract is:

- Planning job emits `has_operations` and an immutable intent artifact.
- Execution job runs only when `has_operations == true`.
- It checks out the bound source, downloads the artifact, validates intent against live semantic inputs, and only then obtains registry credentials.
- A missing artifact is valid only when the execution job was intentionally skipped for an empty intent; otherwise it is a hard failure.

The current composite action cannot express that job boundary itself; the workflow must own it. The composite action should become a thin `plan` / `execute` adapter, not the holder of release semantics.

## Security and correctness work that should not wait on the redesign

Two existing behaviors should be treated as baseline defects in the new design, not deferred “hardening”:

- The publish/tag/release chain has insufficient success propagation. Tag failure is reported but not necessarily made fatal, and GitHub release creation is currently explicitly swallowed with `|| true` ([callisto-action](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/action.yml:212)).
- The durable-plan proposal’s field-source secret check would miss credential-bearing configured URLs. Make secrets impossible in the durable type instead.

For advisory reproducibility, `cargo-deny` already supports configuring an advisory `db-path`, and `--disable-fetch` lets CI ensure it audits a specific prepared checkout rather than silently fetching a different revision. That supports a single wrapper that fetches/records the database revision, then audits that exact checkout ([cargo-deny advisory configuration](https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/advisories/cfg.html)). I would not add a direct RustSec dependency merely to build a competing audit mechanism.

The exception registry should also have one source of truth. A second structured exception file alongside independent `deny.toml` ignores will drift. Either make `deny.toml` the reviewed canonical source with owner/expiry metadata, or generate/verify the cargo-deny section from a single richer source.

## 006 needs a product decision, not another validation rule

The current prerelease model uses snapshot keys that are inconsistent across readers, and bare package-name semantics are intentionally ambiguous in a polyglot workspace. Before implementing “abandoned” or group-conflict behavior, centralize the canonical prerelease member key.

Then choose one model deliberately:

- **Workspace-global prerelease shaping:** fixed/linked groups participate in the normal group calculation, then prerelease shaping applies consistently to all resulting versions.
- **Release-set-scoped prerelease authority:** introduce explicit membership as a first-class model. Do not infer it from `initial_versions` presence.

The current proposed “reject qualifying package” behavior is neither: it leaves difficult cases under-specified and becomes unsatisfiable with multiple qualifying packages. Any validation should aggregate all conflicts into one deterministic diagnostic, not fail on whichever package happened to be visited first.

## Crate choices

I would use:

- Existing `atomic_write` and the existing precondition-oriented model; no new persistence framework.
- `sha2` as a direct, explicit dependency for artifact byte digests if not already direct.
- `serde_json_canonicalizer` only if cross-language canonical JSON is a committed requirement.
- `url` only if raw endpoints remain anywhere that needs structural validation/redaction.

I would not use:

- `cargo_metadata` as release truth: Callisto is deliberately polyglot and already has graph/config semantics.
- A direct RustSec integration alongside cargo-deny.
- `cap-std` as part of this release project. It may be worthwhile for a separate filesystem-capability hardening effort, but coupling it here would obscure the release-state design decision.

## Recommended planning outcome

I would land 005 after its missing cross-glob contamination test is added and after `lint-docs` is invoked by the actual GitHub CI workflow—not merely by local `just ci`.

For the rest, I would not begin implementation from the current split specs. First create one short architecture decision/specification that fixes:

1. intent / receipt / reconciliation boundaries;
2. exact operation identity;
3. source-identity and evidence profiles;
4. registry-reference secrecy;
5. canonicalization and freshness semantics;
6. empty-intent and interruption behavior.

Then revise 001A–C as dependent implementation specs. 002/003 become policy and adapter specs layered on that contract; 004 and 006 can proceed independently after their own semantic decisions are resolved.

That preserves Callisto’s actual architecture rather than making CI artifacts, GitHub shell logic, or an overgrown `callisto-model` the accidental center of the release system.

Don't forget to consider RS best practices, language features in your proposal. We can consider changes, traits, etc. Do we leverage rayon, miette, etc?
Once you've considered all of this present it to me please. I'll share with claude for a second opinion

I won’t suggest crates or traits in isolation from the project’s validation gates and ownership boundaries.

Yes. I understand the process now, and my earlier proposal needed one important correction: it described a target architecture, but did not yet express how Callisto requires that architecture to be discovered, specified, challenged, implemented, and independently proven.

Your process is:

```text
Trace research → Canon accepted spec → Vector challenged plan
→ Lambda TDD + mutation tests + review → independent exit gate
→ Axiom gate before the next artifact/PR stage
```

More precisely:

- Accepted `SPEC-*` files are normative. Semantic-model files describe verified current behavior; plans and handoffs do not override specs.
- `trace` produces evidence and a falsifiable recommendation before a design commitment.
- `canon` drafts, verifies, audits, and exit-gates a spec. A passing spec is persisted and committed before planning.
- `vector` turns that spec into exact, batched TDD tasks and has a challenger test task order, scope, and criterion coverage.
- `lambda` implements each batch red → green → commit, mutation-tests it, reviews it, and runs an independent final exit gate against the on-disk spec.
- A detected architecture mismatch is not “worked around”: implementation stops and returns through `canon/architect` / spec correction, then amended planning and challenge.

That is exactly the process I would follow if asked to implement this. The current “Claude is stuck” report is actually the process working correctly: it found architecture escalations rather than forcing a locally convenient implementation.

## Revised architectural recommendation

Do not make 001A the digest implementation spec. Make the first accepted release spec a narrow architecture contract:

**Release execution is an immutable intent, validated capability, append-safe receipt, and pure reconciliation model.**

The durable state should be:

```text
ReleaseIntentV1 ──validate against live Workspace──> ValidatedReleaseIntent
        │                                                  │
        │                                              ApplyPermit
        │                                                  │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────> ReleaseReceiptV1
                                                           │
                                             pure, non-mutating reconciliation
                                                           │
                                             ReconciledReleasePlanV1
```

This aligns with existing Callisto semantics:

- `callisto-model` owns domain values, JSON contracts, diagnostics, atomic persistence primitives, and capability concepts.
- `callisto-graph` owns workspace/config discovery, dependency ordering, and validation against observed state.
- `callisto-vcs` owns source/tag observations and Git mutation.
- CLI and GitHub Actions are adapters; they must not recreate release policy in shell/JQ.

It also extends an existing Callisto safety pattern rather than inventing a parallel one: `ApplyPermit` makes side effects unrepresentable in dry-run mode ([permit.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/permit.rs:1)).

## Rust shape I would aim for

### Model: durable values only

`callisto-model` should hold serializable, forge-neutral values such as:

- `ReleaseIntentV1`
- `ReleaseOperationId`
- `ReleaseOperation`
- `ArtifactDigest`
- `SourceIdentity`
- `ReleaseReceiptV1`
- `OperationOutcome`
- `ReconciledReleasePlanV1`

`ReleaseOperationId` must be exact: ecosystem-qualified package, registry key, version, and role. It must not use `PackageId::matches`, because that method deliberately implements wildcard-like bare-name matching across ecosystems ([identity.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/identity.rs:13)).

Avoid a generic trait for every concept. Traits belong at real substitutable boundaries, as with the existing `RegistryClient`, `CommandRunner`, `RateLimitPolicy`, and `TimeProvider`. The intent builder and reconciliation logic should initially be concrete graph functions, not `dyn` abstractions invented ahead of a second implementation.

### Graph: validation capability and semantic snapshot

`callisto-graph` should construct the intent from `Workspace` and expose an opaque:

```rust
pub struct ValidatedReleaseIntent { /* private fields */ }
```

Only graph validation can construct it. It should not be `Serialize`, `Clone`, or externally forgeable. Actual publication/tagging requires both:

```rust
&ValidatedReleaseIntent
&ApplyPermit
```

That is better than typestate for persisted artifacts. Typestate is excellent for an in-memory transition capability; it is the wrong tool for JSON that must survive a CI job boundary.

This also avoids the dependency cycle Claude found. `Workspace` uses graph-specific discovery/config state, caches, and non-thread-safe interior mutability ([lib.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/lib.rs:53)); `callisto-model` must not learn how to scan it.

### Serialization and evolution

For a durable, untrusted artifact:

- Dispatch explicitly on `schema_version`; reject unsupported versions.
- Use `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` on each versioned document shape.
- Do not hash an incidental `serde_json` rendering of existing `PublishPlan`, whose optional fields are omitted by serialization.
- Create a dedicated, fully explicit canonical projection for hashing.
- Use `BTreeMap`/explicit comparators and exact sorting rules. Never rely on derived enum order where the wire ordering is part of the digest contract.
- Make the intent’s schema closed, but keep public Rust error enums `#[non_exhaustive]` where Callisto already treats external consumers as forward-compatible. Rust’s `#[non_exhaustive]` specifically prevents downstream code from assuming an API is complete ([Rust Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/type_system.html)).

For cross-tool verification, use JCS/RFC 8785 canonical JSON, not `olpc-cjson`. The latter may produce non-valid JSON according to its own documentation; that is unacceptable for a portable release artifact. [`serde_json_canonicalizer`](https://docs.rs/crate/serde_json_canonicalizer/latest) is a reasonable candidate if the cross-language requirement is confirmed. [RFC 8785](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785.html) should be the normative format reference.

## Security decisions that must be in the architecture spec

1. **Registry endpoints are not durable intent data.**

   Existing plans serialize raw registry/index strings ([plan.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/plan.rs:59)). That can retain URL userinfo or token-bearing query strings. A scan for known environment secrets is defence-in-depth, not a safety property.

   Persist `RegistryKey`, resolve the endpoint only during validated execution, and reject/redact credential-bearing URLs structurally.

2. **Paths in new durable release types must be validated workspace-relative values.**

   Existing model code has a `workspace_relative` validator, but plan entries still carry raw `PathBuf`s. New release envelopes should use a validated wrapper rather than raw paths. This prevents artifact-controlled traversal before a package directory is joined to the workspace root.

3. **Receipt outcomes must be total.**

   Every intended operation must have exactly one terminal outcome: succeeded, already-satisfied, failed, or explicitly blocked/skipped with a typed cause. Absence of a failure cannot mean success.

   The current `PublishReport` only has `Published`, `AlreadyPublished`, and `Failed`, while current downstream filtering treats “not failed” as eligible ([report.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/report.rs:53)). That is precisely why interruption safety needs a receipt model, not extra enum variants pasted into the old report.

4. **Human diagnostics and machine receipts must be separate.**

   Use typed, stable `OperationFailureKind` in durable JSON. Keep sanitized messages optional and bounded. Render user-facing failures through `miette` at the CLI boundary, with Callisto’s normal stable error codes, help, and related diagnostics. `miette` already supports derived diagnostics, source labels, help, and related errors ([documentation](https://docs.rs/miette/latest/miette/derive.Diagnostic.html)).

   Do not serialize arbitrary `miette::Report` values or raw subprocess stderr as durable domain truth.

5. **GitHub approval is an adapter control, not release truth.**

   GitHub Environment protection requires job scope, so the plan/execute job split is necessary for GitHub’s hardened profile. But the core should express source identity and evidence without depending on GitHub types.

   The execution job checks out the bound source, validates the intent, then receives credentials. The workflow should not permit credentials before validation. A failed tag or release must fail the job; existing action handling does not consistently guarantee that ([callisto-action](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/action.yml:212)).

## Rayon, async, and performance

I considered Rayon specifically. I would not add it to this release track.

- Publication must remain sequential where dependency order, rate limits, idempotency, and receipt persistence matter.
- `Workspace` currently contains `RefCell`, `OnceCell`, cached Git access, and generic runner/resolver types without `Send + Sync` bounds. Parallelizing it would require a nontrivial ownership/concurrency redesign, not a one-line `.par_iter()`.
- Rayon reductions/searches can have intentionally unspecified execution order; that is hostile to reproducible diagnostics and canonical durable output unless results are explicitly collected and sorted ([Rayon docs](https://docs.rs/rayon/latest/rayon/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html)).
- Current graph work has already invested in deferred reads and caches. Profile first.

A future, separately scoped performance spec could consider Rayon only for isolated, read-only, CPU-bound work—for example parsing already-collected independent manifests—after proving deterministic collection into ordered structures. It should never parallelize release mutation or receipt transitions.

Likewise, do not introduce Tokio into the core release flow. The workspace’s Tokio use is Moon/WASM-specific. The CLI release engine is primarily synchronous subprocess and filesystem orchestration; forcing an async runtime into it would add complexity without demonstrated throughput benefit.

## How I would restructure the specs

Before changing implementation specs, run `trace` and `canon/architect` for one foundational contract. It should settle, with no TBDs:

1. Intent / validation capability / receipt / reconciliation boundaries.
2. Exact release-operation identity and prerequisite graph.
3. Source identity profiles: Git commit, clean-tree policy, and future hermetic-content profile.
4. Registry-key resolution and no-secret durable-data invariant.
5. Canonical form, digest algorithm, and schema evolution.
6. Empty intent, interruption, retry, and reconciliation semantics.
7. Which actions are valid in a forge-neutral local execution versus a GitHub-hardened execution profile.

Then amend the existing split:

- **001A:** model contract plus graph-built semantic snapshot.
- **001B:** validated execution and total receipt semantics.
- **001C:** GitHub plan/execute adapter topology.
- **002:** source/evidence policy and consumers.
- **003:** GitHub permissions, SHA-pinned actions, environment, and failure propagation.
- **004:** advisory reproducibility as a separate supply-chain concern.
- **006:** after deciding whether prerelease is workspace-global shaping or explicit release-set authority.

For 004, keep `cargo-deny` as the audit authority. Configure and record one advisory database checkout, then run cargo-deny against that exact checkout with fetching disabled; do not add a separate RustSec-based audit engine. cargo-deny supports both a configured advisory DB path and no-fetch operation ([configuration](https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/advisories/cfg.html)).

## The implementation and validation plan

Once the foundational spec is accepted, I would follow your pipeline exactly:

1. `trace` research report, including current-model citations, external crate/API checks, and explicit rejected alternatives.
2. `canon` draft → verify → audit → exit gate. Persist and commit the accepted spec.
3. `vector` plan grouped by crate boundary:
   - model types and serialization tests;
   - graph snapshot/validation tests;
   - receipt/reconciliation tests;
   - CLI adapter tests;
   - GitHub workflow fixture/static tests.
4. `lambda` one subsystem batch at a time, every task red/green/commit.
5. Mutation testing must target:
   - omitted receipt operation;
   - changed source identity;
   - registry-key substitution;
   - stale semantic input;
   - interrupted publish before/after each operation;
   - false “already published” / skipped classification;
   - tag/release attempted without full prerequisite success.
6. Independent lambda exit gate against the accepted spec, followed by an Axiom PR gate.
7. If any batch reveals another dependency-layer conflict or an unrepresentable invariant, halt and route it back through `canon/architect`; do not “finish the ticket” with an unsafe local patch.

My conclusion for Claude: land 005 once its actual CI invocation and cross-glob mutation test are present. Keep 001A/B/C, 002, 003, 004, and 006 out of implementation until the foundation above has passed Canon. The current blockers are not a failure of drafting—they are the evidence that the repository’s process has correctly reached the architecture boundary.

Response from claude:

Verified the load-bearing citations against real code — all check out exactly as claimed: ApplyPermit's capability-token pattern (permit.rs), PackageId::matches' deliberate bare-name wildcard behavior with its own caller-contract warning (identity.rs:122-129), PublishAttemptResult::is_failure/PublishReport::has_failures matching only Failed (report.rs:94-105), and Workspace's RefCell/OnceCell fields (lib.rs:5,53). Nothing fabricated.

Substantively: this is stronger than where I'd gotten to, and I'd defer to it. Specific points where it's genuinely better, not just different:

- The ValidatedReleaseIntent opaque-capability design resolves the crate-cycle problem more cleanly than anything I proposed. I flagged the cycle but left "where does digest logic live" as an open question; Codex's answer — callisto-graph builds an opaque, non-Serialize, non-forgeable type, and mutation requires holding both it and &ApplyPermit — is a real solution, not a workaround, and it's the same shape as the existing ApplyPermit pattern rather than a new one bolted on.
- PackageId::matches being wrong for release-operation identity is a genuinely new finding. None of my reconciliation or gate rounds caught this. It's correct: that method is explicitly documented as an ecosystem-wildcard matcher for human-facing lookups, and using it for exact operation identity would silently conflate packages across ecosystems that share a bare name.
- The receipt-model framing is more principled than my "needs a decision" note on the tag-after-interrupted-publish bug. "Every operation has exactly one terminal outcome, absence of failure cannot mean success" is the actual fix, not "add more enum variants and hope callers update."
- The registry-URL-secret point is real and new. CratePublish.registry: Option<String> — confirmed, raw string, could carry userinfo or a token-bearing query string on a custom index. Nothing in this session's audit rounds touched that.

Two things worth adding to their write-up before it becomes the accepted spec:

1. The olpc-cjson vs. JCS/RFC 8785 tradeoff should be an explicit, argued decision in the spec, not just resolved in Codex's favor by default. Their point is correct — olpc-cjson's own docs say it can emit non-standard JSON — but that only matters if something outside this Rust codebase needs to independently recompute the digest. If verification only ever happens in-process (Rust reading Rust-written bytes), strict RFC 8785 compliance is a nice-to-have, not load-bearing, and serde_json_canonicalizer is a less production-proven dependency than olpc-cjson (already shipping in tough, already in Cargo.lock). Worth having trace settle this against whether cross-language verification is an actual requirement rather than a hypothetical one.
2. Connect 006's open decision explicitly to the bug fix-006-final already found. Codex's "decide whether prerelease is workspace-global shaping or explicit release-set authority" is exactly the bump_target-has-no-roster-check finding from this session (an off-roster package still gets prerelease-tagged in PreMode::Pre because the check that would gate it doesn't exist). Worth citing that concretely in the foundational spec rather than re-discovering it.

Everything else — the Rayon/Tokio rejection, the miette-vs-durable-JSON separation, the #[non_exhaustive] guidance, deferring all six specs until the foundational contract lands — I have no pushback on. Go with it.

Claude’s feedback is well-founded, especially on two things I left too implicit: canonicalization must be selected against an explicit interoperability requirement, and 006 must be tied to the already-observed off-roster prerelease behavior rather than treated as an abstract policy debate. I’m validating those two points against the current dependency graph and release surfaces before I fold them into the proposed foundation.
